utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. If I could just take a few minutes on two matters before the witness testifies, one relating to our motion for binding order against the United States and the other relating to this witness's testimony. With respect to our motion for a binding order against the United States, Dr. Karadzic notes, with sadness and regret, the passing of Richard Holbrooke yesterday, and this will affect our request for a binding order, because one of the items related to testimony that we wanted to use in the hope that we would bring him as a witness in our trial. And I was wondering if we could have leave to reply to the letter of the United States before the Trial Chamber issues any scheduling order so that we could clarify our request for binding order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. In fact, I was about to ask you whether the Defence is minded to withdraw some part of its motion, as indicated by the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think we would be withdrawing one of the requests and perhaps modifying one of the other requests. And it would be helpful if we could clarify that in writing, both to the Chamber and to the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can discuss it in public session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And when do you think you can file it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you could do so, yes, leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Turning to the testimony of Mr. Bell: When we interviewed him on Sunday, we learned for the first time that he had given testimony under oath in a case in Canada relating to the hostage-taking, and that's the subject of Count 11 of this indictment. The Prosecution doesn't have that transcript, and neither do we, and so it's something that we'll have to obtain in the future. I just wanted to put that on the record so that in the event that something in that transcript causes us want to recall him, we would make a motion at that time. I tend to think it's unlikely in his particular case, but it's a recurring problem that we expect will come up many times with witnesses who testified in Bosnia and some maybe in Serbia and Croatia concerning the municipality's portion of the case. And we have a pending motion to order -- or to obtain witness testimonies from national jurisdictions, and we would just make note this problem has arisen in a concrete way with respect to Mr. Bell, and we would hope that the Chamber could assist us in obtaining prior testimonies before witnesses testify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. There's one further matter I wanted to raise which was related to the submission from the parties, the Prosecution and Defence, as regards the judicial notice of authenticity of intercepts. I told the Prosecution to file its submission by the end of this year, but actually what I meant is by the end of the winter recess. And the Defence will have a week from the receipt of the Prosecution's submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but we are actually aiming to file earlier than that, before the Christmas break, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's great. And if the Defence can file it earlier, that would be welcome as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: On another topic, Mr. Robinson, it just occurs to me that if it's possible, where the Defence has had an opportunity to see a witness or potential witness and have an interview with him, and notes have been taken of such an interview, it would be, I think, very useful for all parties if those notes could be transcribed and sent to the witness as soon as practicable after the interview that he or she has had with the Defence to agree the content of them. I think we would resolve issues which might otherwise arise by doing that. There's obviously no obligation on the Defence to do that, but it just seems to me to be a sensible course and is likely to shorten a witness's appearance in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Morrison. After the experience with Mr. Konings, we were seriously considering doing that, and I think we will do that in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bell. If you could make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you just please give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: My full name is Martin Bell.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, you worked as a foreign affairs correspondent for the BBC for 30 years; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, a foreign affairs war correspondent?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: For much of that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, during that time, during those 30 years, and since, I understand you've reported from about 100 countries and 15 war zones; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The prices of inflation, the number of war zones has gone up to 18 now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And among the wars and conflict situations you've covered around the world, that list includes the Nigerian civil war, the Middle East wars, the Vietnam war, the wars in Angola, El Salvador, Nicaragua, the first Gulf War in 1991, and the conflict in Croatia that same year; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from Croatia, in 1991, you moved to covering the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you reported on events there from, as I understand it, the referendum in February 1992, right through until the implementation of the Dayton Accord.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That is true. There were periods when I was out of action. I was briefly wounded, and that stopped me going back for about four months. But otherwise, much of those three and a half years, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And we'll come back to that in a bit more detail very shortly, but now I'd like to ask you whether you recall, in February 1996, giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor regarding your observations and experiences during the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And following that, you also, did you not, testify here in this Tribunal in 2007 and in 2009 as a witness during the trials of Generals Dragomir Milosevic and Momcilo Perisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, finally, do you recall in March 2010 signing a further statement for the Office of the Prosecutor consolidating elements of that previously-recorded evidence we've just been referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, that statement recorded your comments on a number of video-clips, documents, and a map, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did it also refer to passages from a book you wrote on your experiences reporting from Bosnia called "Confessions of a War Zone Thug"?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, the main title was "In Harm's Way," and the subtitle was "Confessions of a War Zone Thug," because I was once called one by a rival producer in Sarajevo, but it wasn't, I hope, serious.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the statement refers to some passages from that book; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you watch each of the video-clips referred to in that statement from March 2010?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did you recognise a large number of those clips as films of your own reports and broadcasts?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, most of them were from my own broadcasts between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in those cases where they were not from your own broadcasts, did you recognise or were you otherwise familiar with the scenes, the situations, and the events that were depicted therein?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them didn't have any voice-over at all, but I was familiar with the events depicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now today, if I was to ask you the same questions which gave rise to the information contained in that March 2010 statement, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, my answers would be exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Your Honours, 65 ter 22275 is a redacted version of Mr. Bell's statement of 8 March 2010, and if I may, I'd like that to be the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Redacted on what parts? Could you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Indeed. Parts that the Prosecution does not intend to rely on: Paragraphs 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To 17?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1996, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, just to go back to your CV for another very short while --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to offer some brief summary of his 92 statement for the public?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was about to do that, Your Honour. Just to go back to your CV for a very short while, I'd like now to read this summary of the written evidence which is filed. Mr. Bell, Martin Bell, was a war correspondent with the British Broadcasting Corporation from 1966 to 1997. He covered and reported on events in the former Yugoslavia from the outbreak of hostilities in Croatia in 1991 through to the signing and implementation of the Dayton Peace Accords. On 9 April 1992, Mr. Bell learned that Zvornik had been attacked by Serb forces. Trying to reach Zvornik that day, he was caught up in a flood of approximately 20.000 Muslim refugees fleeing from the attack. He returned to Sarajevo and, prior to filing a report on this attack, he informed Lord Carrington's personal envoy, Mr. Colm Doyle, who then raised this matter in a meeting with Dr. Karadzic. Mr. Bell was stationed in Sarajevo throughout most of his time in Bosnia and Herzegovina and filed numerous reports on the conditions in the city. Among other things, he observed shelling and sniping in civilian populated areas and severe deprivation caused by shortages of food, water, gas and electricity. Of all the conflicts Mr. Bell has reported upon, he states that in Sarajevo, "there was the least distinction between soldiers and civilians when it came to targeting." Mr. Bell himself was wounded in August 1992 by shrapnel from a mortar while reporting near the Marsal Tito Barracks in Bosnian-held territory. Among his many reports, Mr. Bell reported on the use of a modified aircraft bomb in Hrasnica on 7 April 1995 and the attack on the Markale Market on 28 August 1995. In his view, the staging of the attack on the market would be impossible. Over the course of the war, Mr. Bell conducted interviews with leaders from all warring factions, including the accused, Dr. Karadzic. On 25 April 1992, Mr. Bell accompanied Dr. Karadzic on a tour of positions around Sarajevo. Overlooking the city from a position near Trebevic, Dr. Karadzic confirmed that his forces could take the city at, quote, "any time." In January 1993, Mr. Bell accompanied the UNHCR envoy to Pale to protest the lack of humanitarian access to Zepa. In other interviews with the accused, the discussion focused on territory, maps and history. Mr. Bell and others from the foreign media were cut off from Pale from August 1994 onwards, after the rejection of the Contact Group Peace Plan. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Bell, again to go back to your CV, I have one further question. You indicated in your written evidence and in your previous testimonies that you work as a goodwill ambassador presently for UNICEF. Could you tell us what, as a goodwill ambassador, you do?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. It is an honorary, unpaid job, and I go to the un-quiet corners of the world, countries like Somalia and Yemen, where UNICEF cannot send its real celebrities, and I look at its projects and I return, and I raise awareness of the programmes and I raise money for UNICEF. And that's what the job is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Since leaving the BBC years ago now, have you kept up any connections at all with the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. Bosnia is as dear to me as my own country. I have been back at a number of times. I have shown visitors around. I was once there on a -- on a mission for UNICEF, and only earlier this year I was doing a radio documentary, 30 years after the death of Marsal Tito, about whether he might have been held, at this distance, responsible for the wars that followed 10 years after his death.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I indicated we would come back to your coverage of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina in a bit more detail, and the areas you reported from, and your time spent in the theatre, if we can call it that. Could you set that out briefly for the Chamber? Where were you based and where did you report from?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Initially, we were based in Ilidza, in Serb-held territory. Then partly the reason for that was that the Holiday Inn had been damaged in an earlier attack. When part of it had been repaired, we based ourselves there for quite a while. During the side war between Muslims and Croats from April 1993 to February 1994, I spent much time in Central Bosnia, mostly based in Vitez or Kiseljak. Of course, I visited Tuzla and Mostar from time to time. And when the Dayton Accords were implemented, I was working with the IFOR out of Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You mentioned Ilidza and the Holiday Inn. Are these locations in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, they are both locations in the Sarajevo area. The Holiday Inn is right in the middle of things, between the old town and the new. And Ilidza is -- Ilidza is in -- it was then in Serb-held territory at that side of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Based in Sarajevo, then, could you tell us, roughly, what percentage of your time or what percentage of time you spent reporting from the city?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: From the time I was there, it was -- it was a full-time preoccupation, venturing -- and when I was in the Holiday Inn and, indeed, when I was in Vitez, and sometimes when I was in Tuzla, I did all I could to report from Republika Srpska as often as possible, and I would go to Pale when I could. And I had regular contact with the accused, whom I found most helpful, because I always felt that the key to a settlement of this dreadful war lay very significantly with the Serbs. In fact, I would add that I was regarded by some of my colleagues in the Sarajevo press corps as somewhat pro-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's explore a couple of points that you've just raised, then. You've just indicated that you had -- you did what you could to report from Republika Srpska, you felt that the key to a settlement of this war lay with the Serbs, and you were regarded by some of your colleagues in the press corps as pro-Serb. Perhaps you can tell us, what was your approach, then, to reporting during your time in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, I was not a campaigning reporter. I was brought up in a tradition of balanced and even-handed reporting, and I needed to find out from the Serbs why they were doing what they were doing. And I felt from the start and I have said repeatedly and have written that there was no monopoly of suffering in this war and no monopoly of evil. Dreadful things were done to people, and dreadful things were done by people. And from start to finish, I have tried to be as fair-minded as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to go back to a further point in your answer, where you indicated you did what you could to report from Republika Srpska, could you describe the nature of your access, then, to the Bosnian Serb side of the confrontation lines? How was that achieved?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was achieved by going through roadblocks, and certainly in the early months of the war, that was still possible. I remember one day, even when I was based in Vitez, which is in Central Bosnia, I -- we drove our armoured Land Rover through the Ilidza roadblocks to Grbavica, and there I was welcomed by one of the -- one of the commanders, Mr. Djokanovic, who had been wounded twice in the war. He was a journalist, and he showed me their front-lines. And the point I was making in my report on that day was that Serbs also were targeted by snipers, and Serbs also were victims of the war. And one of the iconic images that stays had my mind is that of a -- of an uphill road in the line of sniper fire. From the other side of the city and across the upper floors of the houses from one side to the other were draped sheets and blankets and rugs to help blind the snipers so that people could move more freely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In order to gain entry to Bosnian Serb-held territory, you indicated you needed to go through roadblocks. Did you need permission from anyone? Did you have any letters of permission, for example?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: At that stage in the war, no. We later needed letters of permission from the Bosnian Army to travel outside Sarajevo or go anywhere near front-lines in Sarajevo. But for the early months, and I would even say the first year or two of the war, we were able to get by -- get through roadblocks just by showing our United Nations press passes and sometimes submitting to being searched.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've just -- in answer to my question about access to Bosnian Serb-held territory, your response was: "We needed letters of permission from the Bosnian Army to travel outside Sarajevo." In order to access Bosnian Serb-held territory, did you need permission from anyone or any organ?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Not at that time. We were, and certainly by 1993, when we reached Pale, we were expected to check in to the Press Centre, which was run by the daughter of the accused, and there we would receive accreditation and ask for facilities, which sometimes we got and sometimes we didn't, but it was quite informal, Ms. Edgerton. I mean, I could walk up to near the Presidency, and one of the accused's assistants would usually come out and talk to us, and over a cup of coffee we'd learn what was going on. Access was reasonable. And from a journalist's point of view, what was remarkable and welcome was that this is perhaps the only war I've been in where we dealt with the main players nearly all the time on the UN side -- and people like the accused were most helpful to us, so was Dr. Koljevic, so was Alija Izetbegovic, so were the HVO, the Croat Defence force in Central Bosnia. We were not mostly dealing with, if I may say so, spin-doctors and spokesmen and with the like, but with the main players.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At any point in time, did the nature of that access to Bosnian Serb-held territory change? Were you cut off?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it did change. We were cut off after the rejection of the Contact Group Peace Plan in August 1994. We were shown the front-lines. We were allowed to interview Bosnian Serb soldiers about why they rejected the peace plan. And then we took our videotapes back to Sarajevo, and that was the -- actually, that was the last time I was able to set foot in Pale, which was -- which was unfortunate for me because it was harder then, having been cut off, to prevent -- to present an even-handed account of the closing year and a bit of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In terms of, then, the type of reports that you and perhaps other members of the press corps in Sarajevo were able to prepare after that time, did this closure of access have any effect?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I mean, there were two elements here. First of all, my editors in London were becoming bored with the war in Bosnia at the time it got into its third year. And, secondly, the Bosnian Government forces became much more sensitive to what's known in the military as field security. They were very sensitive to any video of, shall we say, their mortars firing, their front-line positions, anything that they felt might be of value to an enemy. But this is quite normal in warfare.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What, then -- you've just said it did have an effect. What, then, was the effect on news coverage and news reporting coming from the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think I lamented in my book that the access was confined and all the journalists were working on an access of about a mile and a half up and down the main street in Sarajevo. It was harder and harder to get access. I tried to get access to the front-lines near Tuzla and failed, I couldn't at that time have access to the Bosnian Serbs, and so it was, from a journalistic point of view, a very frustrating time, especially because the war - I'm talking now of the summer of 1995 - was as intensive as it had been in the summer of 1992, but we had less access to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You indicated that you were, as a result of your access to Bosnian Serb-held territory, shown the front-lines around Sarajevo, I presume. Did you have occasion to visit any sniping or heavy weapons positions?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I did. I visited two batteries of mountain guns in January 1993, and, of course, just to take that -- that mountain road to Pale, we were going past front-line positions with armed Bosnian Serb soldiers, and we were -- we were welcome to stop. I mean, they would -- they would give us interviews. They were -- they were very friendly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Were you accompanied by Dr. Karadzic on this or any other visits?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was on -- I was certainly on one visit. He was -- it was, I think, Easter morning, and he was actually showing us the positions and, I would say, making a -- making a peace statement for public and diplomatic consumption, which was perfectly legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we could have a look at your report of this Easter morning visit, and that's 65 ter 40517E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We need to play it again. The witness seems to have difficulty. Okay, thank you. Shall we play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: It was Easter morning by the Serbian Orthodox calender and the Bosnian Serbs were celebrating more widely than they used to in the Communist years. But with a special urgency --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you stop just a second. I'm wondering that is being translated into B/C/S or whether you have a transcript. Did you hear the translation, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, but I was following in English. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Lattanzi also didn't receive the French translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The transcripts were delivered. Perhaps I could just have a moment to speak with my colleague in this regard. We did send the published transcripts around yesterday, so I hope everyone has them. Because there's a number of transcripts, perhaps we may need to hear from the booth that they've found the transcript for the appropriate 65 ter number. So maybe I was a little too hasty to begin playing the film.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Can I get confirmation from the booth?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The 65 ter numbers are not indicated on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I can have your indulgence for a minute, we'll try and find a solution for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, we're minded to take a short break, five minutes, to resolve that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could do that, Your Honour, I'll, with my colleague, work as fast as I can to get this sorted out so that we could proceed smoothly throughout the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry for the inconvenience, Mr. Bell. We need to take a break for five minutes. --- Break taken at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. And my apologies, Your Honour, and my apologies to my colleagues. I think we were all almost defeated by technology, and I think we have solved this for the remainder of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could ask my colleague Mr. Reid, again, if we could try 65 ter 40517E from April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: It was Easter morning by the Serbian orthodox calendar, and the Bosnian Serbs were celebrating more widely than they used to in the Communist years. But with a special urgency to their prayers for peace for their three weeks in to the bloodshed of civil war. All the communities here have suffered. The Muslims perhaps most of all. This village near the airport has been attacked by the Serbs and the Federal Army, its mosque has been blitzed, eight of its people killed, yet today the leaders of Bosnia's Serbs embarked on a peace offensive before leaving for Lisbon tomorrow." "Karadzic: If we didn't have hope for political solutions, we would already free Sarajevo. We would have taken it, because we can take it." "Martin Bell: To make his point, and he did it vividly, Mr. Karadzic took us on a tour of the Serb's front-line positions overlapping Sarajevo. He used an old Serbian greeting, 'May God help you.' The purpose of this high-visibility exercise was to show that the Serbs were observing the cease-fire here and he said, intended to go on doing so. "Karadzic: We don't shoot. We try to just to keep peace and not to -- to control the surrounding of Sarajevo." "Martin Bell: You could take the city tomorrow, couldn't you? "Karadzic: Any time." "Martin Bell: This is the strengths of the Serbs position that Sarajevo lies at their feet. They say that they are willing to negotiate about anything, but if the Muslims want war, they can have war and the city is indefensible. "Martin Bell, BBC News, above Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think the translation of the video is completed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, just a couple of questions about this clip. First of all, do you recall where this position was that you had visited?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. These were the front-lines above Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in the initial moments of this film, you showed Dr. Karadzic making a comment to the effect that they would have freed Sarajevo if they didn't have hope for political solutions. Could you tell us where that was filmed; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think that was when we first met him earlier that morning. We had obviously been with him a little while, long enough for my cameraman to take a ride in his car, where he gave the -- where he gave the Serbian greeting. So it was sort of an ad hoc rolling press conference, if you wish, at the time just before the Lisbon Conference, where he was clearly and, I would say, legitimately on a peace offensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What do you mean, Mr. Bell, when you describe a peace offensive?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was common for all the leaders, especially the political leaders, to blame others for the fighting and to show that they were willing to search for peace and that they wanted peace. If you look at it militarily, I would have thought, for the Serbs to have taken Sarajevo, it would have involved heavy casualties and street-fighting. And Sarajevo, even at the end of the war, there was some terrible destruction, but it could have been flattened as, shall we say, Vukovar was in the -- in the Croatian war. So there was a -- there was always a balance, I think. And I think that the Bosnian Serbs were, from the start, looking for a solution that would be favourable to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To your mind, did the encirclement of Sarajevo have -- by the Bosnian Serb forces have any role to play in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Absolutely. If they could, in some way, bring the city to its knees and more or less get the Bosnian Government to capitulate, then they could have had peace on the best possible terms for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask that this 65 ter number, please, be the next Prosecution exhibit, 40517E?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You will tender only that portion of the video?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, this being also the portion that's referred to in Mr. Bell's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. But the actual videotape, that started in 37 minutes 55 seconds, but when you tender it, you will tender only that part or the entire video?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender, Your Honour, the video as played in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1997, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, you also mentioned visiting two batteries of mountain guns in January 1993, and I'd like us to see your report on that visit. That is 65 ter 40348H. And just for the sake of everyone, perhaps we could have an indication from the booth that they've been able to find the transcript before we begin playing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The French booth has.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: Colonel Jovo Bartula of the Serbian-Bosnian Army commands the big guns west of the city. Earlier in the war, he was named a war criminal by the Bosnian Government, which he resents. He never killed anyone, he says, in his whole life. Now he has it in his power to flatten Sarajevo from five miles away with his 100-millimetre cannon by direct or indirect fire. If it comes to a bombing of the Serbs as some Americans had suggested, his guns would be as prime a target for them as the city is for him. "Are you concerned about the threat of Western intervention? "Colonel: No, that threat only unifies us. Military intervention, all their rockets and planes can't destroy us. The world should understand that we are fighting for the right to self-determination, the right to choose our own state and to live like any other country in Europe." "Martin Bell: Three days earlier, his men had beaten off an infantry attack. Now they are responding with cannon to machine-gun fire. It is an active part of the line, and the UN's role is that of a bystander in someone else's war. Here on the front-line, the prospects for peace seem faint. The war is intensifying between Muslims and Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell -- your indulgence, please. Mr. Bell, do you have any comment on the line of sight into the city from that weapons position, as it was depicted in this film?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Only that I think it shows very clearly how the city was at the mercy of those heavy weapons, whether or not they would be -- would be used. And if they had been used, then Colonel Bartula could actually have seen the impact of his shells and recalibrated them accordingly. And he was outraged, as I remember, to be -- have been called a war criminal, because it was one of the features of this war, Your Honours, that each side tended to regard the military commanders on the other side as war criminals merely because of the position that they held. We had great difficulty persuading him to make this statement, but I think it showed very clearly the mindset of those soldiers and those officers at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask this clip, 40348H, be marked as the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit P1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, I'm looking at -- in fact, I'm quite sure that each of the many war and conflict areas you've reported from was unique in some way. And looking back, I'm wondering whether there is or you recall some feature peculiar to the nature of the conflict as it related to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I would make this point: First of all, it was the centrality of civilians who would inevitably be caught up in a conflict, fought with some quite modern weapons in a modern industrial city. And the other point that struck me at the time is this was probably the first occasion where -- in the history of warfare, where the weapons of mass destruction were used at the same time that we had instruments of mass communication to show the effects of this day by day in the living-rooms of Europe and far beyond Europe. So to that extent, we were, I suppose, participants -- we journalists were inevitably participants as well as witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I asked you to describe the situation for civilians in encircled Sarajevo, as you observed it over time, how would you do that, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would say they were subjected to three and a half years of an appalling ordeal; not all the time. The fighting came and went. Sometimes there were supplies and sometimes -- sometimes there were not. And I would also say it was not just a question of being caught in the cross-fire. There was deliberate targeting also on both sides of the lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, I'd like to turn to an excerpt from a report you did in January 1993 as part of a documentary programme for "Panorama." But before we play that -- and for my colleagues in the booth, that's 65 ter 40348D. Before we play that, I wonder if you could tell us a bit about this documentary programme for "Panorama" and the -- your objective, as you crafted the programme.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: "Panorama" is a long-form series of long-form topical mini-documentaries. It provided me with the possibility of a month of breaking away from the short-form, rushed, rather fragmentary, day by day news coverage, and to spend time with the people, considerable time, to see it from their point of view. There were two other -- in the back of my mind, I had two other objectives as well. I wanted to document, as far as possible, the scale of the killing in the early weeks and months of the war, which was even then not widely known, so there were many interviews with victims. And I also wanted to provide an understanding of the position of the Serbs. The section with the mountain guns and Colonel Bartula also came from that documentary, which included scenes of a massacre of Serbs in a village near Bratunac on the Christmas -- Orthodox Christmas Day of 1993, so it was a complex mix of intentions that I had. But there was so much going on, and I have a wonderful cameraman, and I think that the result was -- it was truthful.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now turn to 65 ter 40348D.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: The casualties are predominantly among the civilians and here first is a sample of what life is like in a city where even the road signs warn of sniper fire. Serbian snipers are perhaps 100-150 yards away in the Kosovo district, where people live right against the front-line. There's no safe place, and lying low in such shelters as there are isn't an option either, for the water is cut off, and the only supply is in the basement of a block of flats. The cellar, itself, is a kind of refuge, but every time they make the journey, which for most of them has to be every day, the water-carriers coming and going are in the line of fire. This day, the snipers have claimed one casualty already and the word from outside is that they've hit another. And the snipers are accurate. Before the war, this used to be a country of hunting, but today [indiscernible]. The victim, this time is a man shot in the leg, just turning the corner when the sniper got him. It happens in this place every day and usually more than once. Nothing special but an everyday hazard for people who have been under fire since April. Our interpreter, who is also a doctor, binds up the wound. Shock is setting in. This is Sarajevo today, Sarajevo any day. He was shot, as one of his companions put it, 'shot for a bucket of water.' It changes nothing for the people of the district. After two casualties in one day, they use the back route which is marginally less in the sniper's sights than the front one. But they still have to fetch their water, and until there's running water and peace, they will have to do it this way. We pressed our armoured Land Rover into service as an ambulance, a kind of luxury for people who, day in and day out, have neither protection nor means of escape from life on the front-line. They tell us we'll be shot at on the way out, and in this sector, that's a fairly safe prediction. "The casualty rate varies from day to day, two dead on a quiet day, as many as 20 under a heavier bombardment, many more injured, not only among Muslims who tend to get much of the media attention but Croats and Serbs as well."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters no longer have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies again, Your Honour. This was a correction to the transcript which was amended last night. If I could just have a moment. Mr. Reid is printing now the correction of the transcript, and I wonder if I could ask it be somehow distributed to my colleagues. And, again, my apologies to them as well, and thanks for their understanding. I wonder if I could ask Mr. Usher to deliver a copy to my colleagues in the French booth. May we continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: There is an everyday price being paid here for the delay in finding a negotiated settlement, and, by and large, it's being paid by the people without guns. This man was still arrive on arrival at hospital, but only just. He died of shock. "Most evenings, the fighting intensifies. Cannon fire here against an office building in what remains of the city centre. The survivors huddle for safety underground. There is no safe place in Sarajevo, but the least unsafe is a cave by the river, once a restaurant, now returned to its function of primitive shelter. Seventy people - all it can hold - have been living here since the siege of the city began."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, I have a couple of questions about this report, and first I'd like to refer back to the scene where someone fetching water was wounded by sniper fire. Was this a situation where someone was, as you've alluded to before, caught in the cross-fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No. The man who was -- who was wounded had clearly been targeted. We could have gone anywhere in the city that day. We just chose this particular example, and we -- and we stayed there. And I have to confess that after all these years, I still find that report quite painful to watch. One effect was that I was subsequently accused by elements in the British Government of being, I think it was called, a founder member of the "something must be done" club; that is, that the images, themselves, called for international intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In terms of the situation for civilians in the city, as you observed it over the course of time, do you find this report of yours to be an accurate depiction?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I'm confident that it is accurate and truthful. There was no fiddling with the soundtracks. You can see the woman wincing when she hears the sniper fire. There was -- this was the worst winter of the war, the winter of 1992 to 1993, and I think that report conveys an accurate picture of the suffering inflicted on innocent people.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have this clip, please, 40348D, as the next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, over the course of time during your time in Sarajevo, did you see any manifestations of a psychological effect on the civilian population of these prolonged conditions?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This is just anecdotal, Ms. Edgerton, but I've never seen such anxiety etched on everybody's faces. They lost weight. I would say some of them looked almost gray with fear. It is -- we had it easy. We came in and out. I would do, at the most, five, six weeks. They were there all the time, with no means of escape and trapped in what appeared to be a war -- a war without end. In fact, the interpreter I used, that wonderful doctor, I believe her father killed himself at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to turn at this moment to a video you saw and spoke to during the course of your Dragomir Milosevic testimony, 65 ter 40425A, from 22 November 1994, a very, very brief clip. But, again, if I could hear from the booth that they've been able to locate the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We haven't been able to find it yet. Bear with us for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: Out on the streets, his UN protection force was actually doing some protecting. A slow-moving armoured personnel carrier sheltering people against sniper fire."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, you commented on this image in your written evidence as being one of the iconic images, to your mind, of the war. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Because it shows, in a very simple form, the fear of the people, and they feel their only safe way - this is quite near the Holiday Inn - of getting across that bit of open ground is in the cover of the French armoured personnel carrier. And I will confess that in my commentary about the UN Protection Force actually doing some protecting, there may have been an element of implied frustration that they hadn't been doing more sooner.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I ask for this as the next Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, I'd actually like to leave Sarajevo for a moment -- a few moments and take you back to one of the first stories you filed from Bosnia in April of 1992, and that was on the situation in Zvornik at the end of the first week of April. Do you recall how you actually came to travel to Zvornik at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. We came from Belgrade, where I had interviewed Zeljko Raznatovic, known as Arkan. And we came to Zvornik, and at that time it was clearly on the verge of war, and I would say that the war there was quite unstoppable. But I do remember doing a report about Zvornik, a formerly mixed town, being on the edge of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we then go to 65 ter 40517B.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while we wait for everyone to find the transcripts, perhaps I could ask you this, Mr. Bell: What gave you the impression that you've just spoken about, that Zvornik was clearly on the verge of war and the war was quite unstoppable?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Because we learned inside Zvornik, at the time when its Serbs had left, that the police force had split, and I think there's a sequence in the coffee shop where the men are talking of the imminence of war. These are Muslim men.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My colleagues in the booth okay if we go to that video now, 40517B.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: All right for the B/C/S booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: French booth is fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: There were reports today of fierce fighting in the ancient town of Mostar in the south of Bosnia between Serbs and Croats. Elsewhere between Serbs and Muslims. Though Sarajevo was quieter today, it seems that the ethnic and political fabric of the republic is coming apart day by day. An example, Zvornik on the Serbian border. It used to be a mixed town of Serbs and Muslims, but in three days 95 per cent of the Serbs have fled. The police force is split and front-lines are being established just as they were in Croatia nine months ago. Centuries of peaceful co-existence between Muslims and Serbs in this town have come to an abrupt end. The war here, says a local leader, can start any day. Bosnians in the old town are angry, frightened, expecting to be attacked. 'The worst can happen,' he says, 'anything can happen.' Others blame outsiders for stirring things up and the failure of their own political leadership. It's their own town and it's as if the prison walls were closing in on them. The Serbs on their side of the lines were taking in suspects for questioning by the busload. The men on guard here were members of the most disciplined of private armies, Commander Arkan's volunteers. They have just accounted for 41 so-called Muslim extremists, in an action in Bijeljina nearby. Mr. Arkan himself is not impressed by Bosnia's peace marshals. "Arkan: The worst thing is that the Communists are back, slowly coming back in power in Sarajevo. You could see pictures of Tito, you could see red flags. They are calling for Communist parties. They are singing Communist songs, and I think that's -- that's wrong, the wrong thing to go 50 years back." "Martin Bell: Zvornik itself was part of Tito's Yugoslavia, but that was a dream that died, and Bosnia is back today, where it was a month ago, on the very brink of war. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Zvornik, Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, is that the report you've just been discussing?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions about this film we've just seen. You noted the presence of Arkan's men, and I wonder how you recognise them to be Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I knew Arkan's men well from the war in Croatia. I had been to their headquarters. I had even done a report on his volunteers being baptised in the great cathedral in Dalj. I knew Arkan well. The interview there was conducted in the ice cream parlour that he owned in Belgrade. They quite often wore balaclavas, as you would have seen in this report, so I had no difficulty in identifying them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You also spoke of an incident in Bijeljina, and you reported: "They have just accounted for 41 so-called Muslim extremists in an action in Bijeljina nearby." Do you recall what information you had about the events in Bijeljina and how you came to be aware of it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The report was -- this report was edited in Belgrade. And when I was in Belgrade, I found out about the attacks in Bijeljina, which actually yielded one of the iconic still images of the war which appeared on the front page of "Time" magazine. But I have no reason to doubt the accuracy of that report and those figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What was that still image you've just referred to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was one of Arkan's men with his foot on the body of one of the Muslims in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have this as the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit P2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, before we move to another clip, we're about one minute short, by the clock on my computer, from our break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, following this report, did you have occasion to return to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I believe it was the 10th of April, 1992. I was trying to do a report on the front-lines around Sarajevo, but I couldn't get access. And then I thought these scenes in Zvornik, let's go and see what -- I wanted to go to Zvornik, itself, because nothing is known of what had happened there. So -- yeah, so I went, and I managed to get, I think, some quite remarkable images on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What were those images?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: They were images, first of all, of the fighting at Zvornik. They came from my very brave Serbian cameraman, Dragan Hercegovic [phoen], and from my camerawoman, Katherine Gisler [phoen], who was with me. We witnessed the flight of Muslim refugees from the area 'round Zvornik in very large numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like now to play that report you've just referred to, which has 65 ter number 40517C.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: Serbian irregulars in action in Zvornik, a town that used to be mixed and used to be peaceful. Today, it wasn't either. These were not men of the Yugoslav Army, but of the most disciplined of the Serbian militias under Commander Arkan. They were mopping up the last of Muslim resistance. The Bosnian authorities, mainly Muslim, were driven out of the town. They put their total dead at at least 300. That may be an exaggeration, but casualties were certainly heavy. The Serbs are now doing in Bosnia what they did last year in Croatia, which is on an argument of self-defence to extend their control into the formerly mixed areas. In fact, they're making Greater Serbia happen. In a village two miles south of Zvornik, we came upon the human calamity, which is the practical result of all this. Two-thousand Muslims are stranded and struggled to get out. They spoke of the fighting they left behind them, the murder and hostage-taking which went on. "But everything are happening now. They have been happening since two, three days. It is a terrible [indiscernible] which has been made and which is being made right now. You can hear even now some shells." "Martin Bell: We could, and so could the refugees waiting for rescue. The artillery barrage was creeping towards us in the villages of the Muslim side of Zvornik. "What is happening," she says, "is we are unarmed and they are firing at us.'" "Martin Bell: He begs the world to help them against the aggression of the Serbs and the federal army. The cry as we leave is again for help as quickly as possible, and the applause is only because we are the first sign they had in days that anyone out there cares about their plight. Numbers are difficult to estimate, but in single file on mountain paths and great columns in the wider tracks, it's possible that as many as 20.000 people are on the move, most of them by foot. [Indiscernible] has been walking for two days, they've gone 18 miles and have at least another 20 to go along this trail of tears. They are heading for the safety of the Muslim area without any help. No food, no medicine, no transport, but all they were talking about was the actions of Serbs in their town of Zvornik." "They killed all peoples. Some peoples from the Serbian forces have something like a wire put on their neck and they pull." "Martin Bell: It is a great and tragic displacement of people, thousands of them being driven from their homes for no other reason than the Muslims are weaker and the Serbs are stronger and the ethnic map of Bosnia is being re-drawn. The refugees are looking for help, to the European Community, to the United Nations and the Commissioner for Refugees. There's not a sign here, of any of them. "Martin Bell, BBC News, on the road from Zvornik."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, I have a couple of questions for you about this report. You referred to your very brave cameraman as being the man responsible for the first part of this film. Do you know where it was shot?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. It was -- it was shot in Zvornik. That would have been the municipal building. And that was certainly Arkan saluting the -- saluting the flag.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You also mentioned the figure of 300 casualties. Do you recall what information you received to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This was information that I received from Dragan Hercegovic, because he then went back to Belgrade and he filed his footage from there. But this was then seen in Belgrade, and Arkan was upset by it and he disputed the figure, and so I then did another report the next day, really to save Dragan from retaliation, making some reservations about the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How did you come to know that Arkan was upset and disputed the figure?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Because Dragan Hercegovic called me that night and told me, and I said I would do what I could to help.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say you did another report to save Dragan from retaliation, what kind of retaliation were you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was speaking of intimidation. They could have beaten him up, they could have -- they could have killed him. And so the next day, I filed a report in which I said the Serbs absolutely deny any massacres of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you said, in this report, that the ethnic map of Bosnia was being re-drawn, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: These were the early days of the war. This was, I think, the first visual evidence we had of what came to be known as ethnic cleansing. I mean, the sheer numbers involved were -- were very great, and this report did have a considerable impact, and, actually, Your Honours, it still does. Earlier this year, I received a letter from a man in Canada who had been the little baby dressed in green, carried in the arms of a man in that great file of the thousands, and this Canadian, he told me that his -- that the man was his uncle, who'd later been killed in the war, and he was grateful, at least, for the existence of this report because it was the only evidence they had of what had happened at that time. And I wrote back to him, wishing to God that the rest of his life could be more peaceful than the beginning of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you bring the matter of what you had seen and reported on in the clip we've just viewed to anyone's attention?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. We drove as fast as we could from Tuzla to Ilidza, and I was editing this footage on the first-floor room that we had, when we saw an official car pull up. And I went rushing down to the reception of the hotel, and it was Colm Doyle, the representative of Lord Carrington. And before he'd even checked in, I took him aside and told him what had happened, and I said I thought he should bring it to the attention of Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not that ever happened?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I believe that it -- that it did happen, though, in fairness, I mean, I just wanted Dr. Karadzic to know what was -- what was going on. These were the -- the fighting, so far as we know, had been done by Arkan's paramilitaries, which were certainly not at any time under the -- under the control of the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How would you know that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Because I knew Arkan. Arkan took orders from nobody, nobody. He was -- he had a very tense relationship even with the -- even with the JNA. Having said that, he couldn't have got across the border through the roadblocks without some collusion somewhere and somebody letting his men across. But, you know -- and, you know, I knew this guy really well. He used to describe me as his friend, which was putting it a bit much. But, no, I knew him really well. I knew his mind, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have this clip, then, Your Honours, 65 ter 4051C [sic], as the next Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you referred, Mr. Bell, to a further interview that you conducted -- a further report that you made to protect or to save your cameraman from retaliation of some kind. Did that report include an interview with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I can't remember where the interview was shot, because by then I believe he'd taken off to Pale. It must have been shot around there at some time. He was no longer in Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall, by any chance, what you might have had to do to arrange that interview?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It may have been shot by the Sarajevo agency pool. It may have not even -- at 18 years' distance, I can't remember, even, whether I arranged it myself. But I certainly didn't need a spokesman from that side to explain their view of what was going on in these very volatile early days of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like now to go to 65 ter 40517D, the report that we've just been discussing. 40517D. I just see, Your Honours, that one of the booths doesn't have a copy. So Mr. Reid will print that up, and we'll make sure they have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: It's estimated here that fighting has been going on in 17 different parts of Bosnia, a number that varies from day to day. Today's hotspot was Visegrad. This is the voice of a Muslim extremist who has taken over a dam on the River Drina and is threatening to blow it up. If he does, it will cause incalculable damage to the valley below, which includes the town of Zvornik, captured by Serbian forces in the past two days. The Serbs insist that the refugees and casualties were on their side, too, although they get less attention, and they absolutely deny the reports of massacres of civilians. What is certain is that every day there are thousands of refugees, Serbs, Croats and Muslims, driven from their homes in mixed communities and seeking somewhere safer. The leader of the Serbs here speaks of Bosnia as being already divided into three." "Karadzic: In Serbian part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is no war, there is no mess, there is no chaos. There is law and order, there is state functioning. In Muslim Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is chaos. In Croatian Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is war." "Martin Bell: In the new and dangerous realities here, it is the civil of all communities who are suffering, and their political leaders, so far from negotiate, are hardly speaking to each other. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, in this video-clip, we heard Dr. Karadzic say to the effect of "in the Serbian part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is no war, no mess, no chaos." What did you understand him to be describing when he referred to the Serbian part of the former republic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I imagined he was referring to what you'd call the Serbian heartlands, rather than to formerly mixed towns like Zvornik, Visegrad, Foca. The reference would have been to the Serbian heartlands.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Those areas -- did you have any information as to what was going on in those parts of the former republic that were ethnically mixed; Zvornik, Visegrad, Foca and elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Not sufficiently. I've always had reservations about broadcasting reports of atrocities, because they can merely make things worse, and if they are unfounded, it's irresponsible. And one of the reasons that in the "Panorama" programme I was talking about earlier we interviewed a lot of victims, it was because in these early days, we had just rumours of what was going on. And when I discovered what actually had been going on, which was targeted killing and people being taken away from some of these communities in buses, and the buses would then be riddled with bullets, what we broadcast in these early days was very fragmentary and incomplete, but it wasn't false.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this clip, please, 40517D, be the next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2003, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, you mentioned, in discussing this last clip, something called the Sarajevo agency pool. What was that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: This was an innovation for which I was partly responsible. The early fighting was so chaotic as the front-lines were established, and there were at that time two principal news agencies -- television news agencies, WTN, World Television News, and VIZ News, which later became Reuters, and their cameramen would compete with each other and offer their material to Eurovision every day, as would we. But for the agencies, there was a -- there was a winner and a loser every day, and they were being impelled by commercial imperatives to take -- in my view, to take ridiculous risks. And so I suggested a meeting of them and us and the other national broadcasters, and we came up with the idea that any material shot by any of our cameras would then be available to everybody. Now, the news agencies in London didn't like this altogether. One of them called the cameraman in Sarajevo and said, Have you guys lost the killer instincts? That's what he actually said. But the case for it was so overwhelming that the Sarajevo agency pool was established by about the 22nd of April, and it -- and it saved lives. And it remained in operation -- this syndicate, if you like, of news agencies, it remained in operation until the summer of 1995, when it was ended by Reuters. I felt it was a constructive and life-saving experiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to play another film clip, then, also drawn from the exhibits in your consolidated statement, 65 ter 40348G.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: In Sarajevo, the horrors are not just heard of, but lived through day by day. This is a particularly heavy bombardment on the old city. A single artillery shell fell on a queue of people waiting to pick up water outside the brewery. Eight were killed, 18 seriously injured. Of the dead, three came from one family, the mother and father who were killed instantly and the daughter who died later in hospital."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, this is one of your reports drawn from the "Panorama" programme in January 1993. But what I'd like to ask you is: Is this a Sarajevo agency pool film?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I believe it is. I can't be for sure at this distance, but the cameramen was on the ground very quickly, and they -- they were in that area much of the time, so I would think it probably -- it probably was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How is it that cameramen were able to be in the city centre, on the ground, as you put it, so very quickly if there was an incident to report on?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, it was their -- it was their business. Most of the -- much of the serious fighting happened between the -- roughly, the Holiday Inn and the Bascarsija, the old town. And, you know, we knew when there might be an up-surge in the fighting, because there often was, just before a cease -- one of the many cease-fires came into effect or when there was a distinguished foreign visitor visiting the Presidency. The Presidency was once rather famously attacked when Mr. Akashi was inside it. So some of these things were almost predictable.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have this 40348G, please, as the next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2004, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bell, earlier today you noted that, based on your observations and your recollection, the war around Sarajevo was, in the summer of 1995, as intensive as it was in the summer of 1992. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like to now play you two of your reports, one from 1992 and one from 1995, and, following that, ask for your comment, please. The first one is 65 ter 40372C, and it dates from June 22nd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: In the two days since the United Nations withdrew from the airport, the city has been under almost constant bombardment. The firing has gone both ways, since it is not defenceless, but we have watched as the Serbs, in effect, walked their mortar fire across Sarajevo and on to the old town. And then at lunchtime today, a round fell directly in the middle of the main shopping street. In spite of everything, people do go out in large numbers at this time of day, and the mortar claimed its victims at random among them. This is the second time there has been an attack of this kind, and it has to increase the pressure for outside armed intervention. Nothing else is working. This was the same street a short time later, the dead and the injured had been taken away, the mortar bombs kept on falling. To say that the daily life of these people is intolerable is understatement. There is no safe place or time. This house was hit last night for the third time. The woman inside had lost her son in the war and saved her grandchildren by minutes when she sent them underground to safety. At the best count we have, there are 52.000 children trapped in this hell hole. "She'll stay where she is. She has nowhere to go and nowhere else to take them." "Martin Bell: The business of Sarajevo is survival. Its people have neither hope of escape, nor thought of surrender. "We are all united here to fight for the freedom of our state, even the children [indiscernible] what's going on here." "Martin Bell: After today's attack, survivors scramble to get on board the one-and-only bus from the city centre. Any lull in the bombardment is a short one. In previous times, there's always been some hope of mediation. Either the European Community Observers were here or the United Nations. Now the EC Observers have gone away, and the UN has suspended most activity until 48 hours passed without any fighting. Forty-eight hours? There's hardly five minutes here. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, do you have any comment that you wish to make on this film from 22 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think it shows quite vividly the helplessness of the people and the extent to which they had been abandoned by the international community. I mean, it shocks me now, looking back on it, to think that the UN should have suspended its activities for 48 hours. It should have intensified its activities. I think it outrageous that this war was left to play itself out for three and a half years. And I've thought a lot about this, Ms. Edgerton, and to me the blame lies also with the -- with the Western democracies, who didn't care enough about the people or understand that everyone's safety was threatened by this fire burning in a part of our common European home.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us how widely reports of yours like this would have been disseminated across Europe and further?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Very widely, depending on the -- on the nature of the report at the time. It was such a dangerous place that many news organisations tended not to send their staff there. But we had a satellite dish first in Ilidza and then at the television station from which reports were sent out all over Europe, usually through the Eurovision news exchange. A lot of my reports were used by the BBC's, similar public broadcasters, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, and my reports were used initially quite a lot by NBC, then when the contracts changed, by ABC of America. So, yes, they went a long way beyond the shores of the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your discussions with the accused, did you ever have occasion to talk about any number of these reports that you had made about the situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think the accused was well aware of these -- of these reports. I believe on one occasion, I don't know if it was one of my reports, there was a report on the BBC 6.00 News that he took issue with, and then quite reasonably he had the number of the BBC 6.00 News, and I believe he phoned. I mean, this was -- this was, in a sense, open coverage of an open war among the people, and I'm sure that he was well aware of what we were reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have this clip, please, 40372C, as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2005, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we move on now to 40511A, a report of yours, Mr. Bell, from June of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: The United Nations here has lost all contact with the Bosnian Serbs, yet the Serbs want to open talks with the contacts group, whose peace plan they have rejected, about the hostages and about security guarantees. This may be an attempt to blitz their way back to the conference table, but they do seek an end to their isolation. "The Serbs are not doing well militarily. They've called for volunteers to hold the line on one battle-field, and near Brcko they've failed in an offensive to widen the corridor connecting the two parts of their territory. They're also responding by tightening the noose on the capital. For the people here, it's like a return to the worst of times. The Serbs have cut off both power and water. The people of Sarajevo have been here before. They have learned to improvise and need all the best friends they can find. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, how was this, to your mind, a return to the worst of times in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Because there was no cease-fire, by the summer of 1995 -- by May 1995, the fighting was intensifying, not just because the Serbs were pressing whatever advantage they had, but because the Bosnian Government forces were seeking to break the encirclement of the city both from inside and outside. I mean, there were offensives. There was some days when we were sure there was a higher volume of fire going out of the city from inside than was coming into the city from outside. And there was one offensive, particularly, in which Bosnian Government forces, up this slope, managed to get across the main road that we used to go from Lukavica, the Serb barracks there, to Pale. It was a -- they were beaten back, but there was -- there was some serious and, I would say, suicidal assaults by Bosnian Government forces. And we knew the extent of them from the many death notices in the newspaper "Oslobodjenje."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you referred to a return to the worst of times, what period of time were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was referring to that dreadful first summer of the war, when so many of the worst atrocities occurred, the level of fighting, the amount of incoming fire. And, of course, that continued through the winter, as you saw with the report that I showed -- you showed from the water-carriers under fire from "Panorama." But the level of fighting was never constant throughout the three and a half years. There were cease-fires, there was the Jimmy Carter-brokered peace deal, and it was as if it followed a pattern that both sides would use a winter lull, say, from December to March to replenish, to re-equip, and to prepare for the coming offensive, and that's what happened in the spring of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This broadcast also referred to Bosnian Serb forces tightening the noose on the capital. What did you mean to convey by that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I mean, when they -- when they cut off the -- when they cut off the gas, when they didn't allow UNHCR convoys through, then they were tightening the noose.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did events in Bosnia -- elsewhere in Bosnia tend to have any effect on events in Sarajevo, to your observation?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think I noted somewhere that events in Sarajevo were like a barometer of what was happening elsewhere, but that may have been wishful thinking, because we were able to travel out less and less as the war continued. But we were aware of substantial changes in the -- in the gap against the Croatian border, when the towns of Grahovo and Glamoc fell. We were aware of an incredibly complex situation in the Bihac area, to which I had no access, but where there were five different forces fighting. And the Serbs were first pushed back, and then they recovered a lot of ground. And the only access we had to what was happening was through their television. In my book, I call it "soldier vision." It was usually shot by a soldier.
