But for us, Sarajevo was, I suppose, always the center of things, because we were -- we were, for long periods, unable to travel out to work and not -- I mean, the most frustrating time, I think, was the summer of 1995, when -- after Srebrenica had fallen, and we could give no account for many weeks of what might have happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could this video, 65 ter 40511A, be the next Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2006, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Bell, I'd like to close with one of your further reports taken from the "Panorama" programme in 1993, and it has the 65 ter number 40348E. And for my colleagues in the booth, that was the last transcript you received.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: Just a year ago, before the war, Sarajevo took pride in its diversity. Mosques, churches and synagogues nestled companionably across the fault lines of two old empires. Now there's more than a city destroyed, a way of thinking too. In place of the old one: Love and let live, is the new one: Kill or be killed. The place has become a city of the dead, as the graveyards advance on the centre. First one park was filled up, then another. Now the dead are buried on a football field, within line of sight of Serbian snipers and easy range of the mortar bombs. The Bosnian Government admits having lost 2.300 of its fighters in the defence of the city, the Serbs at least as many. They, too, have cemeteries filling up under fire. There are no winners here."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you have any comments you wish to make on this last video-clip, Mr. Bell?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. Again, it is a -- it is a reflection and, I'd even say, a lamentation on the war. It was my considered conclusion for the "Panorama" programme. What you're seeing here is virtually the death of a city, or at least you're seeing the death of a city as it used to be, and you could still see the scale of the fighting in the acres of graves. And I've always thought that this terrible war didn't have to happen. It could have been averted. Now, most of what you saw there were the graves of Muslims. If you were to go to the Bosnian Serb town of Sokolac, they've got a -- they've got a very moving cemetery there, where so many -- there are thousands of their soldiers are killed. And I may have got a bit too emotional about it. I tried not to in that report. But I thought then, and I think now, Ms. Edgerton, what a terrible waste of lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's the examination-in-chief, Your Honours. And at this point, I would just ask that those associated exhibits, not already tendered into evidence during Mr. Bell's in-chief, be marked as further Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll first deal with the exhibit that has been played in the courtroom. We'll admit -- we'll give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P2007, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that there are some video footage, the transcript of which does not match with the actual video, so I will ask the Court Deputy or Legal Officer to communicate with you to sort it out in due course. Are there any objections from the Defence? So those associated exhibits that have not yet been admitted will be admitted and given numbers by the Court Deputy and circulated to the parties in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And my apologies, again, for the situation with the transcripts to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Now, Mr. Karadzic, it's for you to cross-examine Mr. Bell.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bell. First of all, I'd like to express my gratitude to you for meeting with the Defence team, and I hope it will enable me to make this cross-examination shorter and smoother. You are, perhaps, my best opportunity, in view of your experience from many wars, to present a picture of the real nature of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That may well be so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thanks. Looking at the list of all the wars from which you reported, some of them are quite similar, others are quite different. There were wars where professional armies were involved, militias, and in others, civilians waged war. Do you agree that the Bosnian war resembled most the war in El Salvador, out of the list of wars where you worked as a reporter?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Karadzic, there's some truth in that, in that it more closely resembled civil wars than it did what the military analysts call industrial wars fought by formations of regular units against each other to achieve a decisive result. But I would go on to say that I think the war in Bosnia was really unlike any other that I have ever witnessed, both for its ferocity, for the difficulties in bringing it to a close, for the lack of distinction between soldiers and civilians, and for long periods I felt that for all the -- that the Geneva Conventions might not have existed, because they didn't seem to apply to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I noted a passage from your evidence, in addition to what you said about the lack of distinction between soldiers and civilians, and that is that civilians were trapped in this war. Let me ask you: Were you aware that a large number of fighting men on both sides, especially on the Muslim side, called today the federation, were waging war in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I believe that certainly happened in the early weeks of the war, when, apart from the JNA, there were no regular formations anywhere, except maybe the Territorial Defence. What we found, as the front-lines solidified around Sarajevo, were groups of armed men, mostly in civilian clothes. But then on both sides, something more recognisable as regular forces emerged. But there were also -- there were armed criminals as well who, I think, used this period of anarchy for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the issue of trapping of civilians, would you agree that restricting movement and transferring civilians into safer areas also contributed to the suffering of civilians and that installing military infrastructure and military targets in civilian areas also contributed to civilian suffering?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Dr. Karadzic, many of the civilians who were able to fled for their own safety. This was the case with the scenes that were shown near Zvornik. As far as Sarajevo was concerned, it became, of course, a city at war. Its established military barracks were both -- used by United Nations contingents. And, yes, any city at war will be a militarised city, but even in those circumstances I can see no justification -- I mean, obviously civilians will be caught in the cross-fire in such a situation, but I can see no justification for either side or any side in any war targeting civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agree on that completely, and we are not trying to justify anything. We will just be trying to understand, and you will be a very precious witness in this attempt to understand what was going on. You underlined another peculiarity of this war, compared to other wars that you witnessed, and that is what you called a deep historical background, richer than in other wars. Did you mean the ethnic components, the components of civil war after the First and especially after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic. I believe that the -- I mean, the history of the peoples of Bosnia is peculiarly complex, and I've written of the Serbs, and I - this is not in any way critical of the Serbs - rather admire them for it. But you live your history like no other people on earth. I mean, you go back to 1389. And, of course, when I first arrived -- when we first met in March 1992, I was pretty well aware of the complexity of the past, especially the wartime experiences. I had already worked, you understand, in the Croatian war, and I was aware of what had happened in the concentration camp at Jasenovac. I was aware of the suffering of your people, and I don't think it would have been possible to operate as a reporter for these three and a half years in Bosnia without knowing a lot about your history before I began and discovering even more as I -- as I went along. And that's said in a most respectful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this. Would I be right in believing that you also came to realise that the anxieties and fears of various peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I'm particularly familiar with those of the Serbs, were genuine and derived from the Second World War, which was not that long ago?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, indeed I do. This was -- this understanding was with me -- was with me all the time. And I came to believe that Tito's attempt to fashion a republic of brotherhood and unity, although it probably became closer to realisation in Bosnia than anywhere else, and I think I'm right in saying there was more inter-marriage in Bosnia, I think it was perhaps doomed to fail simply because of the folk memory of those terrible events in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You took the position that after the events in Slovenia and Croatia, the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina seemed inevitable?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, I have argued repeatedly that -- as Lord Carrington did, that when the European Community agreed to the recognition of Croatia, it made war in Bosnia inevitable. Lord Carrington warned that it could well be the small spark that ignites the powder keg of Bosnia, and yet the European Community agreed to this. And when I lay the blame for what happened beyond the peoples and armies of Bosnia as the war developed, I believe that the Western democracies, and specifically my own government, bear some burden of responsibility. In fact, I can tell you that after I left Bosnia, I fell into politics in the United Kingdom and became briefly a member of Parliament, and this was one of my motivating forces. I thought, If this is how little politicians can do, maybe I can try to do better as a politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you get the impression - and I believe you discussed this - that the rest of Europe and Serbia's erstwhile allies, England and France, succumbed under pressure of other countries to recognise -- to recognise Croatia and Bosnia; they did it reluctantly, but they did it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, this is -- this remains controversial, but I note that the concession given by the British to the Germans over the recognition of Croatia, because the Germans, through Hans-Dietrich Genscher, were pressing for it, that concession coincided within two weeks with a concession by the Germans to the British over the opted-out clauses of the Maastricht Treaty, which were then controversial within the British Conservative government under pressure from its Euro skeptics. And after that meeting, John Major, a decent man, the, prime minister, went back to the House of Commons, having secured these concessions, and announced, in the tennis metaphor, Game, set and match. I think that decision cast some very long shadows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of our interview, I presented to you our theory that Yugoslavia was created in 1918 by our allies, England, France and Italy, and also, in some sense, so that Croatia and Slovenia be taken out from under German pressure. And then later on, Slovenia came under German pressure anyway, and the whole of Yugoslavia later. Would you agree that when Germany's weak, Yugoslavia is created?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before you answer, Mr. Bell: I'm wondering what the relevance of these lines of questions are. I allowed you some leeway to understand the context of the conflict, but I don't see the point of delving into detail. So could you be brief, Mr. Karadzic, on this. Having said that, Mr. Bell, could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I'm qualified to speculate on what happened in 1918.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I prefer to talk about things nearer today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. That was my last question on history. But we really wonder to what extent we are able to decide our own fate, because we are, after all, part of broader politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the short-lived war in Croatia was also able to generate genuine fears among ordinary people in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, I remember that it wasn't so short-lived. It began in June and ended in about February of the next year, and it claimed thousands of lives. But, of course, it destabilised the whole region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But as far as fear is concerned, do you believe that fed the anxiety and fears of ordinary people and inspired them to take measures of self-defence, made them wary of their neighbours, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was clear at that time that Yugoslavia was falling apart, and all its peoples had grounds for great anxiety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to this historical peculiarity and the obsession with history, you noted that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, communities waged war, one against another, there was war among militias and ordinary people, and you could see that even best men killed one another?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic, that is -- that is -- that is certainly true. But there was not, as you -- as we both understand, a total separation of the people throughout the war. I mean, there were tens of thousands of Serbs inside Sarajevo for the three and a half years of its duration. We're not talking about entirely separated communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems you know about it as doctrine of armed people; that is to say, the Territorial Defence, which was organised for the contingency of some attack on Yugoslavia from the east, and you were aware that there were large amounts of weapons distributed across municipalities, and even companies and businesses, all within the concept of All People's Defence. Was it, indeed, your theory that Bosnia was quite well supplied with weapons and did not need any imported?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There is two pretty distinct questions in there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Shall I ask the accused to break it up, or would you be able to answer the question, having the benefit of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll answer it -- answer them briefly. I'm aware of the Territorial Defence. I'm aware of the existence of arsenals within Bosnia. It was -- and I'm aware that especially Central Bosnia was the arms-producing centre of Yugoslavia. In Vitez, they made dynamite. In Bugojno, they made land-mines. I don't think this is in dispute, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, refrain from asking compound questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm trying to save time, but to my own detriment, it seems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that you were quite able to distinguish between periods of presence of the Yugoslav People's Army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and its role, and periods after the JNA left?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. It was a confusing time, but it was a very swift transition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that up to the 20th May, the date of the pull-out of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Territorial Defence was in place, as well as self-organised groups, without any centralised control or command?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I would -- I would -- I would agree to that, the self-organised groups with all three of Bosnia's peoples, but most of the -- most of the weaponry was accessible to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now view a video that could perhaps help illustrate this subject. It's 1D2885. I hope transcripts exist. No, they don't?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "There are paramilitary people in the city who are under nobody's control, and they come from all ethnic backgrounds. And they have to come under somebody's control, because they, together with others, are destroying the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it consistent with your knowledge and your position? Did you make this film?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I rather remember making this. I think it was in Ilidza, and I accept entirely what Colm Doyle was saying there at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this be received, this clip?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D916, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that all the way up to the 20th of May or later, there were not enough opportunities to gain insight, let alone control, over the developments on the ground; I mean, primarily the events in Zvornik? Is it true that we were hardly able to find out what was going on, let alone control it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, those were the very -- the very early days. There was no Bosnian Serb army in existence at that time. The Bosnian Government didn't have its own organised army, neither did the Croats. This was part of the anarchy of the early days of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were based in Holiday Inn, and, to the best of your knowledge, there were many crews based there, over 50 crews of the largest news agencies?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would be surprised if there were as many as 50, Dr. Karadzic. Some came in and out briefly, but those who stayed for the duration were the Sarajevo agency pool, CNN, ourselves, the Germans and the French. And I wasn't actually based in Holiday Inn until towards the end of June 1992, because, as you know, it was partly destroyed in some earlier incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that time, we met, you and I, in the Serbian part of Ilidza. Do you remember that we both had offices in the same hotel and held press conferences there?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I remember it vividly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall one attack by Muslim Green Berets, who fired even at your hotel where you were staying, although they were not targeting you deliberately, but they were firing at the Serbian part of Ilidza? I believe that was in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that attack vividly. In fact, I had a bullet pass very close to my head and bury itself in the wall behind me, which I dug out and put in my pocket as a -- as a sort of a good luck mascot. And a friend of mine, an agency cameraman, was quite badly wounded in that attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I noticed that you acknowledged and appreciated the way we treated you and that you were able to access Serb territory, but also the main players, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was a very unusual experience for me, and I did appreciate that, that access and your hospitality, sir. And I very much regret that for the last 15 months of the war, we had no access to you or your headquarters or your staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that during the first two years, you could travel around Republika Srpska without any escort from us, just by virtue of the fact that you were accredited?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. If I had tried to get to active front-lines, I -- there were -- there was one time you gave me an escort just to be helpful. But, no, when I visited Republika Srpska at that time, the greatest difficulty -- hazard I faced was actually driving across the airport runway, which was like a -- like a free-fire zone. Once I got to Lukavica, I was safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the establishment of government and control and the state organism of Republika Srpska was, in a way, a green-field project, as it were? Without institutions and without infrastructures, we started establishing law and order and the rule of law?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, clearly there was -- there was a rule of law within your heartland, I mean, Banja Luka, Pale, the Romanija Plain. I don't expect to find the rule of law in a war zone on active confrontation lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is from that point of view that I was wondering whether you had noticed that the worst days and the most terrible crimes occurred over those two months before June, and that later on, as some kind of control was being established, the number of crimes went down. Does that tally with your own observations?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need some reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's just really rather vague and broad right now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can manage an answer, if it's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, it is a matter of record that some of the very worst crimes of deliberate murder were committed in the early weeks of the war; not the only ones, but some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could comment on the last part of his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Does that tally with my observations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a limited area in Sarajevo. But we didn't find out about some of the worst crimes actually for many weeks or months, because they were hidden and they happened far away from any journalists, any UN, any anything. It was a time of anarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, your observation was that the JNA in Sarajevo played a constructive role and that they were not to be blamed for what was happening in Sarajevo at first while they were there; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: When the war began, I remember there being a plan for joint patrols between them and others. I knew General Kukanjac. I am not sure the extent to which his heavy weapons may have been involved at some stage. I was in the main street where -- in the early days where there was certainly some incoming either artillery or attack fire, so I don't know where that came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were speaking about the possibility of having a war avoided altogether, did you have in mind the offer of the European Community concerning the reconstruction of Bosnia into three ethnic republics, well known as the Lisbon Agreement or the Cutileiro Plan, the Carrington/Cutileiro project, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I had in mind, first of all, what might have happened if Croatia had not been unilaterally recognised so early, but, yes, I remember the Lisbon Conference as a time of hope, and I wish it had succeeded because so many lives would have been saved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I please call up 1D2881. Could I have in e-court, please. It's a video-clip which will help us illustrate -- or, rather, establish what it is that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: The Serbs here are on the defensive, but holding the line, the front-line, situate this morning to the west of the city, an area of hotels set in parkland which had been the secure headquarters both of the European Community Observers and of the foreign press. Our morning call came from the barrel of a gun. Many guns on both sides. This is a mainly Serbian enclave, and it seems that the Muslims, emboldened by their relative success in the city center late yesterday, were attempting to storm Ilidza today. They were met with stiff resistance by the Serbs. It was a battle of fire and movement in which the Serbs were trying to improve their positions tree by tree across the front-line. It was also dangerous, obviously, for the photographers. The veteran VIZ News cameraman, Rob Seliers [phoen], who shot these pictures, was the furthest forward and paid the penalty for it. He was taken to an army hospital, then flown to Belgrade, where he is now safe. It was, up until this point, the federal army's only involvement in the battle. "An 11.00 a.m. cease-fire dead-line came and went, and the fighting after it was, if anything, fiercer than it was before. There is no mediation, there are no peace talks, only Serbs and Muslims battling it out; yet the would-be peace-makers were here on the spot, a dangerous one. They included the personal envoy of Lord Carrington, who is due to visit tomorrow. " "Lord Carrington: We have to consider whether or not it is safer at this stage for this important visit to take place." "Martin Bell: Or if the will for peace is here." "Lord Carrington: We don't know whether it is at the moment. We made a lot of appeals. The situation is very serious. We are not too sure what we're going to do at this stage." "Martin Bell: The battle lasted for a full 10 hours. Only then did it begin to subside. The Serbs had held their positions, but at a cost which both sides are still counting. One of the Serbian soldiers told me how three of his comrades fell fighting alongside him. "My cousin -- two of my cousins, and one of my best friends. I have [indiscernible] to God, but it was very bad."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this to be the Command of the 2nd Military District in the center of Sarajevo that was attacked even before May by paramilitary groups, the Green Berets and so on? Is that that area?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I recognise it as the hotel where I was based. And, of course, I remember this whole scene very vividly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is proof of how fierce the fighting was, in actual fact, when the JNA had already decided to withdraw, and there was fighting going on involving them as well?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: If I reported there was no JNA involvement in this, except the evacuation of the cameraman, that is true. The ferocity of the fighting is not in doubt, and I think this video-clip gives a very particular demonstration of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please play 1D2883.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That transcript for that video that we just saw is largely incomplete and contains a great deal of inaccuracies. And because it's an English transcript, one can easily see that by following along with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The problem is that the -- we have English sound, but which cannot be, in full, translated into B/C/S. But the accused is bearing with it. What would be your suggestion, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I was actually also thinking about the translation of that transcript into French, because it's important that Your Honours have an accurate record of the transcript. I would ask that if they propose to use this, that they revise the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Is there a way, on the part of the Defence, to provide the transcription of this video-clip, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, after -- after this is admitted, we will certainly have it transcribed in English, but at this moment we were not in a position to do so. We were hoping that it could be heard and interpreted, since the sound was quite good. At any rate, we are going to have it transcribed, and we will submit the transcript. Can the clip be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit it. But in the meantime, we will mark it for identification until the time we'll get the English transcription.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D917, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I just make one further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I should have risen earlier, but a date, even approximately, to the events depicted would be useful, I think, for all of us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can give you the date, sir, if it's of any help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there. It was the 22nd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fantastic. Thank you, Mr. Bell. I note the time, Mr. Karadzic. It's time to have a break. We'll break for half an hour and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I please have 1D2883.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, I would like us to see what those first days looked like while there was still hope that peace would be established. Fortunately, you were there, and you saw for yourself everything that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: There has been a gun battle going around this hotel in the parkland all morning, but [indiscernible] it hasn't stopped, its fight intense. We've now been told that rather the European Community Monitoring here have been warned that this place is targeted for incoming mortar fire sometime around now. So it's not a very comfortable situation, but I can assure you, from personal experience, that there is no cease-fire here. That is a hard line [indiscernible] to say. I'm sorry, it's a little bit disturbing, some of this noise. The Muslims are in a very difficult position, geographically, and the Serbs have to [indiscernible], and the Serbian Army have them surrounded. On the other hand, the Muslims fought back strongly yesterday, and as far as I can tell what's going on around here, it's a fairly -- it's a fairly even match."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the hotel at Ilidza, and are you on Serb territory here?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is that hotel, and I am on Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your assessment was that this was a fairly even match; right? That's what you say towards the end of this report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it seemed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there is no doubt that as for this Serb part of Ilidza, the Muslim group of the Green Berets was attacking from the other part of Ilidza; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time they were Green Berets, but certainly the Serbs were under attack from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is also around the 22nd of April, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is possibly the -- possibly the morning after. It was the day that bullet nearly hit me and it hit the wall behind my head.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it bear the same 65 ter number as the previous one, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the way it should be. I don't think that that is the case. I think this should be the next day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was mistaken on that part. But I'm wondering whether we should mark it for identification as well, Ms. Edgerton, for the sake of transcript. Do we need -- we need the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Again, I'm just thinking of the translation of this into French, if Your Honours are going to be giving it consideration.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it can be MFI'd until we provide a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it when the translation is done, so we'll mark it for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D918, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I meant "translation" to mean transcription of this video, not necessarily the translation. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Muslim armed groups felt rather self-confident at the time and that they even attacked the JNA itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first part of that question calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could you reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that from the very outset, there were numerous groups, Muslim groups, that were armed and that were in town?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: There were certainly armed Muslim groups, and there were armed Serb groups which appeared to me in many cases to be completely ad hoc, so they had improvised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that at first the JNA was expected to be between the two parties and prevent the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: That was my understanding at the very beginning, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now play this, the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise the man that you see on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber who it is?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It looks to me like General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Can we play the video now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: 'This army is staying in Bosnia-Herzegovina,' he said, 'We are withdrawing from certain areas, especially those most under attack, but we will continue to be the army of the people who shelter and accept us.' Outside the rumour, he was talking about the evidence of the most recent attack. His headquarters in the old part of town was shot at again last night. This is an angry general. 'Mortars, rockets, snipers, bazookas, heavy machine-guns.' He listed the weapons used against the headquarters and produced the evidence, what he called his souvenirs, along with a warning against whoever might try it again. 'If we are attacked, we shall retaliate fiercely.' He read from what he said was a declaration of war by the Croats and the Muslims, led by President Alija Izetbegovic. The army until now has been more neutral in this war than it was in Croatia, but its patience is strained. It was moving today to the Serbian side of the lines and taking its big guns with it. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Sarajevo." "Martin Bell: So at the very gates of army headquarters this evening is the United Nations armoured car carrying President Izetbegovic. This is where the deal holds together or falls apart. The soldiers were already rushing to get out of the headquarters, and President Izetbegovic was present, if not as a hostage, at least as a most reluctant guest." "[Indiscernible] negotiation, negotiation in UNPROFOR." "Martin Bell: He exchanged meetings with an army that he believes is an occupying force and spent some time with its general, while the troops continued to load up and get out. Under the deal, the two men would then have gone their separate ways but Bosnian Television tonight showed the argument that started when the convoy was stopped at a Bosnian roadblock. 'We have an agreement,' said the president from inside the armoured car, and both men got through, but nine of the army's vehicles were highjacked, there is no peace. And much of the city is shattered. "Martin Bell, BBC News, Sarajevo." "Martin Bell: In the wards where some of the ten soldiers wounded when the army convoy carrying their commander to safety was stopped late yesterday by Bosnian forces, nine vehicles hijacked, more than 150 soldiers captured. By the army's account, four of its men were killed, including two colonels shot in cold blood in this ambulance. General Kukanjac was still within sound of gunfire at his new headquarters and angry. 'Nothing like it will happen again,' he said, 'because if we don't settle this, we will act differently.' From Slovenia to Croatia to Bosnia, the federal army, the army of the old Yugoslavia, has taken a battering. Culminating in the damage to its Sarajevo headquarters last weekend, the forced evacuation, the ambush of a convoy with 100 soldiers captured and we now know 14 killed."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but I just want to rise on one point. I've been sitting here with Mr. Reid and can see quite clearly that at least one part of this video has been included in the associated exhibits from Mr. Bell's amalgamated statement. And I wonder if it's at all possible, as we go on, if we can be informed of the time codes or ERN numbers from which these video-clips are taken, as we did in our initial notification, to avoid the Chamber being unduly burdened with duplicate -- duplicative evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are on that issue, can I revisit -- not "revisit." It's about the transcription. The video we've seen as part of an associated exhibit, are there -- the transcript of those exhibited or what's the status of those exhibits? I can't find them in the e-court. All I can find is just a surrogate sheet, a one-page surrogate sheet. So we should have marked them for identification as well, then, if we follow the rule. But it is there?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I was just advised they're attached as translations to the original surrogate sheet. But, indeed, Your Honour, I'll double-check that for you, because given the experience of this morning, I'm sorry to say that may not be the case with all of them. But we'll certainly look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It was, yes, as translation. Thank you, we got it. I think I can find it. Yes, it's there. Thank you. Now you have the answer to the question posed by Ms. Edgerton, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I believe that in our list, in our notification, there is a reference to the origin of each and every one of these clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, there's no time code references, Your Honour. That's the thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Bell was kind enough to inform us about Ilidza, the 22nd and the 23rd of April. As for this, we are going to provide the time reference to the OTP. Oh, you meant the minute code references. That's what you meant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I thought you wanted to know what the time of the actual occurrences was. We are going to provide you with this. We are just going to specify what it was, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I propose to carry on, and that overlapping problem could be sorted out in due course outside the courtroom between the parties, with the assistance of the Registry. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall now like to call up in e-court 1D2806.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, do you like to tender that piece where we could see General Kukanjac?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask Mr. Bell: You saw that the JNA staff was under attack for a while, and the JNA was preparing to withdraw from Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with what Kukanjac said, that from Slovenia through Croatia, and now in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in some areas they were seen as the enemy army and suffered many blows?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: They certainly suffered a blow when the agreement to exchange General Kukanjac and his soldiers for the semi-captive Alija Izetbegovic broke down, and I don't think there is any doubt that some of those soldiers, especially the ones in the ambulance, were killed in cold blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you also remember that there had been attacks on the headquarters even before, and the day before, the JNA hall was attacked, killing several soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. That is why General Kukanjac showed us what he called his souvenirs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 1D2806, please. This is already in evidence. It's a conversation between General Kukanjac and General Mandzic on the 21st April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, we'll -- I take it the 65 ter number of the previous clip was 1D2884. I need the confirmation. I see the nodding. That will be admitted, while marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D919, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how can it be shown here? I was advised that we do not have this one in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope we do have a translation. This is an intercept of a conversation between General Mandzic and General Kukanjac. No, there is no translation. But it's from the 21st of April, and they are discussing what is going on in the city. They are discussing attacks from both sides of the Miljacka River. Can we see the next page. I will read what Kukanjac says: "I called both Koljevic and Karadzic, and also all these Muslim leaders, Come on, Muslims are shooting from Hum, they're shooting from Crni Vrh, from Marin Dvor, from Zlatiste. The other ones are shooting from Vraca. These raided an area in town. It's horrible."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Serbs were in Vraca, and in these other neighbourhoods there were Muslims? Do you recall these localities that I mentioned: Hum, which is a hill, the one on which the TV relay is Crni Vrh, Marin Dvor, Zlatiste - they were held by Muslims then - whereas Vraca was held by the Serbs? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Is this a question to me? I was -- I note there was very heavy fighting in Sarajevo on that day. The exact positions, I didn't know. I was caught up in the middle of it, in the middle of the city, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you were aware of this fierce exchange of fire and this chaotic fighting that these two people are discussing?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Very much so, yes, I was aware of that. I was in the middle of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are about to see -- in fact, I'm going to read out -- the next page, please. I will read out the whole sentence. Kukanjac says -- the next after this. The last sentence in this passage: "That directive of Alija Izetbegovic is being implemented." We need to see the top of the page. It's the last sentence in the first box: "That directive of Alija Izetbegovic is being implemented."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You had perhaps heard of some directives, but you were not sure they existed. Do you remember that on the 12th of April, a directive to attack the JNA was issued, and it was renewed in the end of April?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No. On the 12th of April, I was describing the battle for Kupres. I was not aware of any directive at the time. And, of course, it would have been useful to know, but I was not aware of these directives or, indeed, of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted as an MFI, pending translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was not admitted, as indicated, earlier on. Ms. Edgerton, what was it you wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just don't think there's enough on this intercept for it to be admitted through this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness was not able to confirm anything about this conversation, and as to the general condition, he testified on his own. So I don't think we need to admit this. We'll not admit this through this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, although the conversation between these two generals confirms what Mr. Bell had noted as fierce and balanced fighting. Can we now see 1D01258, please. This is a directive, and for this one, we have a translation, issued two days after the conversation between the generals, and that's the second directive in April to attack the JNA. Please look at the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They define enemy forces, and the JNA is proclaimed to be one of the enemy forces, along with Serb territorial units in Serbian areas, in Serbian autonomous provinces. Can we see the next page in English, number 4, where it says: "I hereby decide ..." Paragraph 4: "I have decided ..." And then it goes on to order a general mobilisation of the entire Territorial Defence and joint command over this entire operation against the enemy, as they say: "Immediately capture weapons and ammunition depots, cut off barracks, capture them, and detain members of the JNA on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And now could you look at number 5, the tasks. From your experience and knowledge, were the events that started on the 23rd of April consistent with what you see in this directive?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, of course, I was not aware of this directive at the time. It was issued on a day where Lord Carrington had succeeded in brokering a cease-fire. But I would have been surprised, in view of the ferocity of the fighting in the two previous days, if there had not been an attempt to seize weapons and co-ordinate a fighting force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's true that you could not have been aware of it, because it's a written military secret. It was not in the public domain, but it was sent to Muslim military forces. Could you please look at Point 6, "Support for Combat Operations." The next page, please, and in Serbian. "Command and Communications." In English, we need the next page after this. All this that you see here, does this look to you as a comprehensive order for an all-out attack, well co-ordinated and well commanded?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Of course, I had no sight of any internal documents of any of the fighting forces. It looks to me like an attempt to establish a properly co-ordinated fighting force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you see number 7: "Immediately set up a command system in the following levels: Unit, municipal staff, district staff, Republican Staff ..." In Serbian, we need the next page. This was sent to municipal and regional staffs and signed by Commander Hasan Efendic. Now, would you cast your mind back to the events of the 2nd and 3rd of May. This was 10 days after this directive. Do you see a logical connection between this directive and what happened in the first days of May?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: There was certainly very heavy fighting in Sarajevo on the 2nd of May. I believe that was the day that the trams stopped, and it lasted all day. I had no way of knowing, from my position on the ground, how it began, but I believe that an attack on the Dom Armije, the officers' club, was part of what happened. And I know this because we were threatened when we tried to get our cameras near it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You surely knew that there was an agreement between the JNA and Izetbegovic that the JNA would pull out from Bosnia, and that had been agreed in Skopje already at the end of April. Do you know about that agreement between Blagoje Adzic and Izetbegovic in Skopje about the JNA pullout from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, and I was aware of the proposal for the exchange of Kukanjac for Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's D222, Your Honours. It's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was. But at a later stage, in a decision dated 30th of September, we denied the admission. It was shown to Colonel Colm Doyle, who was not able to comment on this at the time. But given the answer by this witness, I'm asking your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I think it's a slightly -- I was just reading the comments that Colonel Doyle had given in respect of that document, and I think the situation here is different, in fact, and I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be now admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D920, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at another video-clip, 1D2882.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Instead of giving a new number, we are going to reinstate the old number. So this will be admitted finally as D222. D222, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2882.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said yourself that you witnessed frequent iterations of peace offers for the benefit of your TV station; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. And, Dr. Karadzic, the cease-fires came and went with great regularity, and few of them lasted very long.

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: ... Sarajevo. On board, a jet of the Portuguese Air Force and on a mission as difficult as any in diplomacy, to bring to a complete halt the fighting that had raged in the city for the previous two days and to re-establish a peace process between leaders who at this point were not even talking to each other, so little security and so little understanding that he had to hold separate sessions with them in a restaurant at the airport which is under federal army control and, therefore, the only safe place in Sarajevo for negotiations. The first point, a real cease-fire was perhaps the easiest to agree to, the hardest to enforce. The leader of the Bosnian Serbs was among those committed to it. "Karadzic: We have to sit down at the same table, even in help to even get some peace for this country."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this report? You were present when the delegation arrived, the Portuguese foreign minister and Lord Carrington; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and you were accompanied by Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this video-clip be received?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can advise that's -- that clip is completely subsumed within 65 ter 40526B, which was an associated exhibit to paragraph 61 of Mr. Bell's amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we don't have to admit it separately. Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I should like to display 65 ter 30655. It's an intercept between me and Professor Koljevic of the 4th of April, 1992, two days before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Doyle -- sorry, Mr. Bell. At the time you were in Kupres, do you remember that on the 4th of April, the evening of the 4th of April, Mr. Izetbegovic declared general mobilisation in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I was -- I was carried by a JNA helicopter to Kupres on the 14th -- on the 12th of April. On the 4th, I was not yet in the country, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Let me show you this intercept now, where I am talking with Mr. -- with Professor Koljevic, who was a member of the Presidency, alongside Izetbegovic. We see it on the screen, and there is a translation. The next page, please. The next page in both versions. The first three boxes from the top, I ask what happened at the Presidency, and Professor Koljevic explains that the Muslim side demanded a mobilisation of the Territorial Defence: [In English] "... so I said that there has to be a difference, if we are in the favour of peace or the continuation of the political fight. I told them that this move is politically negative, and, you know, we were in the conflict again, they are continuing their political fight." [Interpretation] If I may remind you, at that time the Lisbon Agreement had already been accepted, and two days before its expected ratification, Mr. Izetbegovic declared all-out mobilisation. Do you agree that this must have been intimidating for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I can see why you would wish to introduce this as evidence at this trial. I would prefer to comment -- reserve my comments to things that happened and statements that were made and battles that were fought while I was actually in your country.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would probably be disinclined to receive this at this time. Can we call up 37 -- sorry, 30714. This is my conversation with Radovan Pejic from the police, who was at Vraca at the time when you were there, the 23rd of April, at the time of that heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you help us with this video?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you need that B/C/S version on the monitor? If you have a hard copy, we can collapse that and zoom in further, for Mr. Bell's convenience, on the English version. Let's do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, I agree. I don't need the Serbian version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those are those critical days, and I'm calling and asking whether that is Vraca. If you remember, Vraca is a Serb neighbourhood above Grbavica, opposite the Holiday Inn. Do you remember Vraca?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's where the headquarters of the Serb police was. Now I would like you to focus on this conversation. The fifth part from below, Mr. Pejic is saying there are some indications that they keep getting organised down there in Grbavica. As you remember, at Grbavica there were both Serb and Muslim armed groups at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now I think we can actually look at the next page; the next page in English, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Pejic is informing me about the fact that there were attacks and that the Serb police was just trying to be prepared if there is another attack. And I say: "All right. Today, a cease-fire should be signed, so we should not start in any way and they should not, as such." Does that correspond to your knowledge regarding my attempts to preserve the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It certainly corresponds to my recollection of the situation on the ground at the time, that after two days of heavy fighting, one in the city and the other in Ilidza, itself, it was much quieter on the day that Lord Carrington arrived to try to broker a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. There is another page as well, and Mr. Pejic is informing me that the headquarters were bombed. Can we have the next page? Ah, yes, I see it here. Windows, yes. The windows were shattered, there was damage from shells and so on. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But not for the -- it has been our practice, unless one of the participants testified, we mark it for identification, pending that issue will have been resolved.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D920, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're on the subject, peace efforts, that is, I would like to remind you of your own statement from 1995. Or was it 1996? If you have it in front of you, or maybe I should read it: [In English] "... first visit to Pale. Outside the Hotel Panorama in Pale, we filmed Karadzic saying, 'If we didn't have hope for political solution, we would already have freed Sarajevo. We would have taken it because we can.'" [Interpretation] End of quote: [In English] "Easter Sunday morning April the 25th, Karadzic took us around his front-lines at Trebevic. He invited us to tour his troops. We saw troops. They were in uniform, as I remember, with a red tag -- batch of badges. Most were in JNA uniforms. There was a cease-fire at that time, and he wanted to show us how his people were observing it. We got the impression Karadzic was fairly popular with his troops. He said he could take Sarajevo at any time, but it was all bravado," as you said: "What they could have done was flattened Sarajevo, as they did Vukovar, but they didn't. They believed it was their city."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Several times you confirmed that we considered Sarajevo to be our own town and that there was not the kind of destruction that had happened in Mostar, Vukovar, and elsewhere; right?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I would [indiscernible] that. It was a shared city in which you all lived together.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't know whether this statement of Mr. Bell's from 1995 or 1996 has been admitted already. Or should we tender it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it has been admitted, because we admitted only his amalgamated statements, but I remember having heard that from a video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would be happy to have that statement admitted, too, because Mr. Bell's memory was quite fresh at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the 65 ter number of it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we're going to find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We don't have it up-loaded, so it doesn't have a 65 ter number for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then it should be added to the 65 ter list, first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can understand the Office of the Prosecutor, the fact that they don't like this statement, but it's invaluable because it was given right after the events concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But as for the contents of this statement, the witness confirmed, and then it's in the transcript. And we heard your voice directly from the video. But if -- yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just a couple of things. I can give you a 65 ter number, although we haven't up-loaded it. It is 09981, and now it's up-loaded. And that passage that was just discussed is at paragraph 43 of Mr. Bell's consolidated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you have no objection of admitting that statement of Mr. Bell's?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. It will be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: With the Exhibit D921, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only difference is that in this statement of 1996, there is that reference to bravado, but that is not of crucial importance. While we're on the subject of cease-fires and attempts to establish an early peace, 1D2886, could we have a look at that now, please. 1D2886. Maybe -- ah, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Martin Bell: The Serbs are continuing their public peace offensive. Their leader, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, sent a letter to 'The Times' this morning with a copy to the BBC, saying that he would court-martial any of his troops who broke the cease-fire. 'We were persuaded,' he said, 'to take a significant risk in the hope of peace.' We will see today if his orders are being obeyed."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this correspond to your knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. I was not -- I was not given to speculation, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Pursuant to that principle, we'll mark it for identification. Or is it subsumed in another --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we move on, and I can respond to you on that in a couple of minutes. It just takes me a little bit of time to check these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's leave it there, and then let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You noticed, yourself, that you were not -- that we were not very skillful at media warfare, as it were, but we were always available for contacts, weren't we?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: With respect, Dr. Karadzic, I think you and your vice-president were both quite good at media warfare. You made yourselves available, you made your case clearly. It was only later in the conflict that we lost sight of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, what I meant was that we had not sufficiently publicised other things we did. Do you know, for instance, that we were establishing a military judiciary at an accelerated pace and that we were trying persons who had committed crimes against Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I did not know that, and it would have been very helpful to have known that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I advise you on this last video-clip that I just asked for a couple of moments on. That was 1D2886, and that's subsumed within 65 ter 40526C, which is an associated exhibit to paragraph 75 of Mr. Bell's amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we don't have to admit it separately, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that a great deal of publicity was given to prisoners of war, and it was that summer, the prisoners of war that were held by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: As I remember, there was a great deal of publicity given to prisoners on both sides, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that the prison for prisoners of war at Manjaca was established as far back as the time of the war in Croatia and that it was established by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, of course, in the time of the war in Croatia, I was in Croatia and not in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the attacks against the JNA, say, in Samac and Western Bosnia, all the way up until the 20th of May, that the JNA had its own prisoners of war and that they were put in the prison in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'm not sufficiently well informed about that, Dr. Karadzic, to be able to help you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now view a video, 1D2887. It has to do with prisoners of war. 1D2887.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Karadzic: Yes, we would accept that. It would help us to quit those prisons for war prisoners." "Reporter: So you would make speedy access possible, say, by the United Nations Commission on Human Rights?" "Karadzic: Anything that comes from the UN, we are going to receive and be co-operative on that field." "Reporter: So if they put people on the ground there tomorrow, those camps would be opened to them?" "Karadzic: Absolutely. We are seeking for the possibility to quit all those prisons by changing all war prisoners all for all, but the Muslim side, unfortunately, don't accept it. But we would accept international help in any kind." "Reporter: Well, we're talking here of international and independent supervision of the camps." "Karadzic: Sure, absolutely." "Reporter: That sounds like the United Nations running the camps. Is that acceptable?" "Karadzic: Yes, absolutely acceptable." "Reporter: Britain is also talking at the Security Council collecting evidence, so that those responsible for any abuses can be caught, tried and punished. Will you co-operate in that?" "Karadzic: Absolutely, we will do our own investigation for our own, because we also want to see whether there were some abuse or not." "Reporter: But if crimes were carried out, if the picture turns out to be that of treatment incompatible with civilised behaviour in the conventions of war, would you co-operate in what would amount to war crimes trials?" "Karadzic: Absolutely. If there are any evidence about that, we are going to co-operate and to help if it comes out clearly." "Reporter: Dr. Karadzic, you made it quite clear that you accept the moves being made by the UN to run the camps, to punish abuses, but to what extent are you able to deliver that?" "Karadzic: I think we are able to deliver anything. If some people are disobedient, we are going to arrest them, as we have already done with some disobedient people." "Reporter: What is the motive for agreeing to these UN moves? Is it to head off the threat of international military intervention, air-strikes against your people?" "Karadzic: No, military intervention means not too much. It would not resolve anything. It would just make this war worse, and it would make this war lasting longer. We just co-operate with the UN because we are right, and we want everything to be settled down proper way. And we think that UN is very helpful for us, for Serbs in Croatia and for Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we manage to inform you about my order of the 13th of June? It was repeated on the 19th of August it had to do with observing International Humanitarian Law and the Law of War. Did you know that before this interview and before the intervention of the United Nations and the Red Cross, we had already set that norm?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I would be grateful for the date of the interview we've just been seeing. Do we know when that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was in September 1992. We don't have the exact date. But, at any rate, it was after that that -- actually, do you remember that by the 12th of December, all prisons for prisoners of war were disbanded and that they were taken to third countries, to a very large extent?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The difficulty I have with this, Dr. Karadzic, is -- for this is this is mostly the period when I was out of the country because I had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was hoping that the distinguished Ms. Edgerton would help us with the date, because we got that in relation to your statement, this intercept -- or, no, it's a video-clip. It was received in relation to what it was that you were supposed to be speaking about. That's the way it seems to me, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's your interview, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, V000-3327-10 -- or, rather, "-A." It's part of that. Would that help establish the coordinates, V000-3327-1? We received it from the OTP. It's most certain that we did not get it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I could help on that, I would, Your Honours, but I can't. I have no idea of the date of the interview, and our records don't give us any date either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Bell, you don't remember having heard that interview by Mr. Karadzic at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I do not, but that's probably because I was in hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have for a moment D101. Could we please have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, on the 13th of June, you were certainly in Bosnia, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was -- give me just a second. I do have -- I do have the records here. It was about the time I returned. My successor had been -- can I say he'd left in a hurry under mortar on the second week in May, and I had great difficulty in getting back across the airport. Probably about the 15th or 16th of June. I have a record here that I did a report on new fighting in Sarajevo on the 17th, and we normally like, in our business, to hit the ground running, as we say, so I would have -- I would have filed as quickly as I could, so I doubt if I was there on the 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, I'd like to draw your attention to this: This is a repeated order. Look at the first sentence, once again: "I hereby order ..." And there are four paragraphs here related to observance of humanitarian law, and there is a reference to the first order that was issued in June 1992 that has to do with the treatment of prisoners of war. So that was before anybody's intervention. That is why I said that, that perhaps we were not active enough and skillful enough as regards the media. Otherwise, these orders would have been given great publicity and you would have known about them. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, absolutely, it would have been very helpful for me at the time of my return, on about the 15th or 16th of June, to have been aware of this order and the many other things you were doing. I think it was an admirable order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm aware of the fact that we, ourselves, contributed, in part, to our failure in the media. Can we just have the next page, please, in both versions. The next page: "The general position: "The Army and the police in the area of responsibility are being issued an order to carry out vigorous investigations." Do you agree that after taking the Serbian municipalities in Krajina, the Muslim police found documentation and investigation material with regard to each and every incident when the Muslims and Croats were victims before the end of the war in 1995, and that to this day proceedings are underway in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the basis of our files compiled at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Again, I wasn't aware of this, and I wish I had been. And I do not doubt, Dr. Karadzic, that it reflects credit upon you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. D95, could we have that for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that our position was that villages, Muslim villages, Croat villages, should hand over their weapons, should not fight, and that we guarantee full freedom to them, as well as safety and security? There is a telegram here that I sent on the 14th of July to the municipalities in Podrinje, that is to say, the eastern part of Bosnia. You, yourself, had realised that it was not under the control of the central authorities. Could you please focus your attention on this telegram now?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.
