utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I would like a reference to support Dr. Karadzic's latest assertion as to what Mr. Bell had said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think he made reference to Mr. Bell's statement earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He said, at page 94, line 19: "You, yourself, had realised," referring to the Podrinje, "that it was not under the control of the central authorities." So I'd like a reference to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not a question asking whether he realised it at the time of the situation instead of his making a statement to that effect? English is not my native --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not good at it most days either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bell, can you answer the question? Had you realised that it was not under the control of the central authorities, the eastern part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think some parts were and some parts weren't. One of the municipalities here is Han Pijesak, which was Serbian -- Bosnian Serb heartland throughout, but I've got -- you know, English is my native tongue, and I've got lost down the judicial byways of the last five minutes, and I'm not entirely sure of what I'm being asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Nothing quite so obscure as judicial byways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic, on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you: Do you know that this really happened this way at Romanija, and around Han Pijesak, and around Rogatica, there were villages that surrendered their weapons and remained safe until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'm very pleased to hear that, Dr. Karadzic. I think the record suggests that something other happened, for instance, in Foca. Or is it in Foca that you met resistance, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm actually talking about villages closer to the Drina River, villages that had surrendered their weapons. And during our interview, it was said that we cannot find a single Serbian village in Muslim territory which meant the year 1995 safe; whereas we can find a lot of small towns, hamlets and villages that were Muslim populated in Serb territory, such as Janja, Bosanski Dubocac, Bosanski Kobas, and then other villages that surrendered their weapons that did remain safe in Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm very gratified to hear that. We -- for various logistical reasons and because of the heavy fighting in and around Sarajevo, we were not able to return to the Drina Valley for a long time. I certainly do remember a Serb village in Central Bosnia, close to the confrontation line between Muslims and Croats, from which the Serbs had fled entirely, and that supports your general thesis here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying to find your statement, or was it perhaps something you said during our discussion, where you said that Karadzic or the central authorities does not have enough control in Eastern Bosnia, but let me read something you said during your interview: [In English] "... a sense of history or mission. He was not a man with hatred in his heart. He would be very surprised -- I would be very surprised if Dr. Karadzic ordered crimes or shooting." [Interpretation] Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I think the phrase about hatred in his heart came from an interview with Nermin Tulic in Sarajevo, who is a very distinguished Shakespearean actor, and he had been taught by Dr. Koljevic. And he lost both his legs in a mortar attack, and what he later told me, that what troubled him was not so much his incapacity for life but he's got something worse than cancer, he said, he had hatred in his heart to those who had done that. As far as the situation in the Drina Valley is concerned, certainly in the early days all regular military forces who were later to engage in the war were in the process of organising themselves, and any central commands and control was extremely fragmentary, if it existed at all. And if I could just add, Your Honours, my view of the war from the start was it was a war among the people, being reported from among the people. I was down there in the middle of them from start to finish. And whether any of the leaders had hatred in their hearts is for them to decide. I was concerned with effects from start to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that we refreshed our memory of the visit by an ITN crew to Trnopolje in Republika Srpska? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes, we did. And, of course, I was not there, but they were, but I'm very well aware of the incident and the affect that it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that I offered that crew transportation by a government plane and gave them free access to Republika Srpska and any location in Republika Srpska they wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: Yes. My friends at ITN have confirmed that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember there was some talk among them that they had found nothing, they didn't have a story, and then they created a story out of the material they had, a story that ended up doing us a very bad turn?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: It was certainly a story that went 'round the world. I know it was -- it was very controversial. I actually -- when I was a member of Parliament, I pleaded with the editor of ITN not to sue the magazine that printed certain allegations. As for the accuracy of the report, not being there, and I'm not really able to comment on it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that somebody from the ITN, Penny Marshal or someone else, told you that they did not have a story and that they made one out of the material they had shot?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: No, that is not -- I forget who told me this, but it was not that. It was that it was only when they got back to their hotel, and looked at their footage and their notes, that they realised what they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you believe, and we will try to show that here, that that crew entered a compound surrounded by barbed wire, and that's how they photographed refugees in Trnopolje camp, as if they, the refugees, were surrounded by barbed wire, rather than the camera, thus creating the illusion that we were holding them prisoners? Was that the enterprise of this magazine called "Living Marxism," an attempt to refute the ITN report?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: The article by Thomas Deichmann in "Living Marxism" was certainly an attempt to refute the ITN report. I think it's for you to show and make your case. If I had been there, I could have been helpful. And if I'd done that report, you'd, no doubt, have me pinned against the witness box. But I can't really speculate about something second-hand, about something that occurred when I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm, again, on the verge of self-criticism, in the sense that we were not very good at public relations, but I hope you were aware that we were opening up completely to the international media and that is precisely how the liberation of most of POWs came about by the end of December. Now I'd like to show 1D2888, a video-clip. Do you agree that we gave access both to the Red Cross and foreign media and foreign reporters, complete access anywhere except, of course, the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: And until August 1994, obviously. But when incidents happened like that ITN report, I think you tended to close up and say, All the foreign press is against us, which had unfortunate consequences, because I was neither for you, nor against you. I just wanted access to find things out, and I had -- and I'm not making any complaints about the access I was granted up until October -- August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your book, on page 100: [In English] "... light, the Serbs were in the grip of extreme spy-mania, and at their roadblocks journalists were doubly suspect for being foreigners - therefore, historically anti-Serbs - and for travelling from the other side of lines." [Interpretation] Do you agree that these searches and suspicions were not insolence on their part; it was, as you say, fear and misgivings that spies -- that spy work is going on, that spies are at large?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I have absolutely no hard feelings about this at all. In a war zone, I expect to be stopped, I expect to be searched. I was a little bit surprised on one occasion when my -- one of your roadblocks, we were stopped, and everything went through, and my Italian producer had a -- had a cuddly toy, a teddy bear, which then had its -- was ripped in two by a bayonet to make sure it wasn't hiding anything. I think the -- I think the searches, especially Rogatica, were probably a little bit over the top. But in principle, I expect to be -- I expect to be stopped, I expect to be searched. And, Dr. Karadzic, after all these years, no hard feelings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as a psychiatrist, I wanted to make a distinction between insolence and heavy-handedness and fear, and a conviction that may arise out of that fear. Can we now play this video. This is a visit by Lord Ashdown, who was not a lord then, to Sarajevo, one of the prisons in Sarajevo. He had also visited Manjaca, but I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reporter: The Bosnian Serbs had challenged him to come and see things from their perspective, and Mr. Ashdown took up the challenge, which began with an extremely unpleasant hour-long helicopter journey. To avoid fire from the ground, the aircraft flew fast and low, a taste of war-time conditions for Mr. Ashdown and those accompanying him. The destination was Pale, the former skiing resort near Sarajevo, where the Bosnian Serbs have a military strong-hold. There, Mr. Ashdown met and discussed his programme with the man who'd invited him, the Bosnian Serb leader, Radovan Karadzic. "Karadzic: And in Sarajevo, there would be no single fight." "Reporter: The visit got underway soon afterwards at Kula Prison Camp, on the outskirts of Sarajevo. Mr. Ashdown was able to talk freely to the inmates, Muslims who said their life was not tough here, but they were not beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know about this prison, Kula, near Sarajevo, and that it used to be a prison for a long time before the war?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN BELL
utterances.text: I'd heard about it, but I did not visit it in person.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have time for an extension today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to conclude for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this video-clip be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to note on the transcript, it shows Martin Bell as being the speaker on the video, and that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you who the speaker was, if it's of any help, Your Honour. It's another correspondent called Justin Webb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. But having said that, you have no objection? We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D922, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bell, we'll adjourn for today and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of December, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.29 p.m.,
